newsitem.title: USA: Budget bill could boost phone rates, critics warn.
newsitem.headline: Budget bill could boost phone rates, critics warn.

text.p: Budget legislation nearing final passage in Congress could inadvertently drive up local telephone rates in rural areas that depend on subsidised phone service, lawmakers and local carriers warned Tuesday.

A group of Senate lawmakers Tuesday sought to delete a provision from the proposed legislation that would divert up to $4 billion to the Treasury that normally goes to a federal fund used to keep phone rates affordable for residents of sparsely populated communities.

Phone companies typically must spend far more to serve customers in hard-to-reach rural areas than those in cities. Money from the "universal service" fund is used to subsidise carriers for the cost of serving these people.
The diversion would occur in fiscal year 2002, with the Treasury slated to reimburse the fund in 2003. The bookkeeping is designed to help balance the budget by 2002.

"While this is a gimmick, it will have an actual effect on universal service support in 2002 and could result in an increase in phone rates in rural, high-cost areas that rely upon the high-cost fund," 16 senators said in a "Dear Colleague" letter to colleagues.
"This provision, which was contrived by the Congressional Budget Office, is totally dangerous in our judgment and this budget gimmick ought to be deleted from the bill," it said.

The senators, many of whom represent large rural constituencies, included Byron Dorgan, Democrat of North Dakota, Jay Rockefeller, Democrat of West Virginia, Republican John McCain of Arizona and Republican Conrad Burns of Montana.
"I don't know of anyone who thinks this is a good idea," said Ken Johnson, a spokesman for Representative W.J. "Billy" Tauzin, a Louisiana Republican.

Johnson said congressional leaders are banking on the hope that federal auctions of the airwaves will bring in more money to the Treasury in the coming years than anticipated, negating the need for the universal service measure.
"The problem is that if the auctions don't (generate the income), we'll be in a real fix," Johnson added.
Local phone companies already have objected to the measure, warning that it could produce "a dramatic rate increase for millions of rural Americans."

"Delaying expenditure of universal phone service support funds will make the system insufficient to preserve universal telephone service as mandated in the 1996 Telecommunications Act," said Roy Neel, president of the United States Telephone Association, made up of the regional Baby Bells and other local carriers.
